entries.answer: A variable is a named container for a value. You put something in it, refer to it by name later, and can change what is inside. In modern JavaScript you declare with let, which can be reassigned, or const, which cannot. Scope decides how long the name stays visible, and getting scope wrong is one of the most common sources of bugs.

entries.answer: A function is a reusable block of code that takes inputs, does something, and returns a result. The inputs are parameters, the output is the return value. Functions exist so you write something once and reuse it, and so each piece of a program does one job you can name and test on its own.

entries.answer: The frontend is what runs in the browser and that the user sees: layout, buttons, styling. The backend runs on a server the user never sees - it holds the data, checks permissions, does the real work, and sends results back. Splitting them lets the same backend serve a web app, a mobile app and an API at once.

entries.answer: A type system is a set of rules about what values a program may hold and what can be done with them, and in statically typed languages it is a compile-time discipline rather than a runtime one. Its value is that whole categories of bug become impossible rather than merely unlikely. The honest cost is verbosity and a real learning curve, and the honest benefit is that a typed codebase is navigable because a function's contract is written down.

patterns: what is an object in programming
difference between an object and an array
entries.answer: An object is a collection of related values bundled under one name, and it is the basic unit of organisation in most languages. In JavaScript objects are also the basis for arrays, functions and dates, which is why the language is sometimes described as having one data structure. The practical consequence is that almost nothing is deeply immutable, so a function that mutates what you passed it is a common source of bugs.

patterns: what is an off by one error
entries.answer: A loop repeats work until a condition fails, and the interesting part is always the exit condition. A loop whose condition never becomes false is an infinite loop, and one that stops one iteration early is an off-by-one, which is why the boundary is worth stating in terms of the first invalid value rather than the last valid one. The most common bug is mutating the thing being iterated, which behaves differently in every language.

entries.answer: Recursion is a function that solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of the same problem, and every recursion needs a base case that stops it. The call stack is what makes it work, since each call pushes a frame popped when it returns, and the practical limit is how deep that stack can go. Recursion is clearest for problems that split, like trees and sorting, and usually worse than a loop for plain iteration.
